lead: The sinc pulse satisfies Nyquist's zero-ISI condition, but its spectrum is a perfect rectangle. A rectangle cannot be built, and its slowly decaying 1/t tails turn a small timing error into interference at the next sample. The raised cosine pulse rounds the corners of that rectangle with a cosine roll-off controlled by one number, α, between 0 and 1. It pays a known extra bandwidth and gets tails that die as 1/t³. The eye pattern is the oscilloscope picture that shows whether the shaped pulse is still clean where the sampler fires. DSL, cable modems and every mobile baseband use this daily.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the zero-ISI condition, the sinc pulse, and the meaning of symbol rate R_s and symbol period T.

sections.h3: From a brick-wall spectrum to a cosine roll-off

blocks.text: In 5.1 the fastest pulse with zero ISI is the sinc, and its spectrum is a perfect rectangle: flat up to R_s/2 hertz, then nothing. A perfect rectangle needs an infinite, non-causal impulse response. No circuit builds it, and a real cable would chop its corners anyway.

Nyquist's criterion allows the corners to be rounded, provided the transition band is odd-symmetric about R_s/2. The raised cosine spectrum does exactly that. It is flat from 0 to (1 − α)R_s/2, then falls smoothly, like half a cosine, to zero at (1 + α)R_s/2.

blocks.where: B is the baseband bandwidth in hertz, measured from zero to the highest frequency used; R_s is the symbol rate in baud, equal to 1/T, with T the symbol period in seconds; α is the roll-off factor, also called the excess bandwidth factor, with 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.
the extra hertz spent above the Nyquist minimum, in hertz; α and R_s as above.

blocks.text: Two extremes frame the choice. α = 0 returns the sinc and the Nyquist minimum B = R_s/2. α = 1 gives B = R_s, double the minimum, with the smoothest and most buildable spectrum. Practical links sit between: a DSL line on α = 0.25 pays 25 % extra bandwidth above the Nyquist minimum and buys a filter that can actually be manufactured.

sections.h3: The pulse in time, and the root raised cosine pair

blocks.where: p(t) is the pulse amplitude at time t seconds; T is the symbol period in seconds; α is the roll-off factor; sinc(x) means sin(πx)/(πx).

blocks.text: At t = 0 the pulse is 1. At t = kT (k ≠ 0), p(kT) = 0; where the denominator also vanishes, take the limit. At t = ±T/(2α) the ratio cos(παt/T)/(1 − (2αt/T)²) tends to π/4, so p = (π/4) sinc(1/(2α)).

The tails decide practical success. A sinc falls off as 1/t. A raised cosine with α > 0 falls off as 1/t³. Sample 10 % of a symbol late and the raised cosine contributes almost nothing, while the sinc still contributes visibly.

The pulse the sampler sees is the cascade of transmit filter, channel and receive filter. Matched-filter theory (see 5.5) says the receive filter should match the incoming pulse to maximise signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant. Both demands are met by splitting the raised cosine: put the square root of its spectrum at the transmitter and the same square root at the receiver. Each is a root raised cosine (RRC) filter. Two RRC filters in cascade give exactly the raised cosine, so zero ISI plus matched filtering for free. An RRC filter alone is not ISI-free; only the pair is.

Pulse shaping is judged on an oscilloscope. The eye pattern, also called the eye diagram, is made by triggering the display on the symbol clock and overlaying the received waveform for two symbol periods, over thousands of random sequences. The traces pile up into a shape with a clear opening, like an eye.

items: Vertical opening: the gap between the worst-case top and bottom traces at the sampling instant. It is the noise margin; noise beyond it causes errors.
Horizontal opening: how far the sampling clock may drift, in time, and still hit an open eye. It is the tolerance to timing jitter.
Slope at the zero crossing: a steep crossing gives a wide horizontal opening, so the eye tolerates more timing jitter. A gradual crossing narrows the opening and makes the eye timing-sensitive.
A closing eye means growing ISI — from a channel that cuts high frequencies, a wrong α, or a clock firing at the wrong instant.

blocks.text: The sampler must fire in the middle of the horizontal opening, where the vertical opening is widest. An eye monitor keeps checking that instant. Raising α shortens the tails, so the eye stays open over a wider range of sampling phase, at the price of bandwidth.

figure.caption: Data becomes a root raised cosine pulse, crosses the channel and is matched by the same filter at the receiver; only the cascade is the raised cosine whose eye is watched at the end. Notice that no single filter block is a raised cosine by itself; only their cascade is.

spec.title: Where the raised cosine is made
spec.aria: The data passes through a root raised cosine transmit filter, the channel and a matched receive filter, so the overall pulse seen by the sampler is a raised cosine whose eye is measured at the end.

examples.question: A binary baseband link carries 4800 bit/s through a raised cosine system with roll-off α = 0.5. Find the symbol rate, the symbol period, the Nyquist minimum bandwidth, the actual bandwidth and the excess bandwidth. State what α = 1 would cost on the same link.
steps: The data is binary, so one bit rides on each symbol: R_s = R_b = 4800 baud.
Excess bandwidth = B − R_s/2 = 3600 − 2400 = 1200 Hz. Check: αR_s/2 = 0.5 × 4800/2 = 1200 Hz, same value.
With α = 1, B = 2400 × 2 = 4800 Hz, that is 1200 Hz more than the α = 0.5 design.
examples.answer: R_s = 4800 baud, T = 208.3 µs, minimum bandwidth 2400 Hz, actual bandwidth 3600 Hz, excess bandwidth 1200 Hz; α = 1 would need 4800 Hz.
examples.check:
Rs = 4800.0
T = 1 / Rs
alpha = 0.5
Bn = Rs / 2
B = Bn * (1 + alpha)
excess = B - Bn
B_alpha1 = Bn * (1 + 1)
print(Rs)
print(round(T * 1e6, 1))
print(Bn)
print(B)
print(excess)
print(B_alpha1)

traps: Choosing α = 0 because it is the narrowest. The sinc cannot be built and its 1/t tails flood the sample under a small timing error. Practical links use α near 0.2 to 0.5, and exams want that justification, not a minimum.
Dropping the half: writing B = R_s(1 + α) or excess = αR_s. Correct forms are B = (R_s/2)(1 + α) and excess = αR_s/2.
Expecting one root raised cosine filter to give zero ISI. Only the cascade of transmit and receive RRC gives the raised cosine; each alone does not.
Reading the eye at its widest point on the picture instead of at the instant the sampler actually fires, and forgetting that the eye is taken after the receive filter, not at the channel output.

quiz.q: Define the roll-off factor α and give its range.
quiz.a: α is the fraction of the Nyquist minimum bandwidth R_s/2 spent as excess bandwidth in a raised cosine spectrum. Its range is 0 ≤ α ≤ 1; α = 0 is the sinc and α = 1 is full roll-off.

quiz.q: Why is the raised cosine preferred over the sinc in a real link, although it needs more bandwidth?
quiz.a: The sinc has a rectangular spectrum needing an infinite non-causal impulse response, so it cannot be built and any channel truncation destroys its zeros. The raised cosine has a gradual, realisable spectrum and tails that decay as 1/t³ instead of 1/t, so small timing errors and channel filtering cause far less ISI. The extra bandwidth αR_s/2 is a controlled, known price.

quiz.q: A raised cosine system runs at R_s = 2400 baud with α = 0.35. Find the bandwidth and the excess bandwidth.
A binary link sends 9600 bit/s with α = 0.25. Find T, the minimum bandwidth and the actual bandwidth.
quiz.a: Binary gives R_s = 9600 baud. T = 1/9600 s = 104.2 µs. Minimum bandwidth = 4800 Hz. Actual B = 4800 × 1.25 = 6000 Hz, excess 1200 Hz.

quiz.q: An eye diagram shows a wide horizontal opening but a small vertical opening at the sampling instant. What is the likely cause and what is not the cause?
quiz.a: A small vertical opening with a wide horizontal one points to amplitude trouble: additive noise or amplitude distortion, not timing jitter. Timing error would shrink the horizontal opening and steepen the effective crossings. If the vertical opening closes as more traces are added, ISI from channel low-pass shaping is the other candidate.

quiz.q: Why does a system use two root raised cosine filters rather than one raised cosine filter at the transmitter?
quiz.a: The receive filter should be matched to the incoming pulse to maximise signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant, and the overall cascade must be a raised cosine to keep zero ISI. Splitting the spectrum into two square roots satisfies both: each RRC filter is the matched filter for the other, and their cascade is the raised cosine. One raised cosine filter at the transmitter alone would leave the receiver unmatched and would be corrupted by channel noise.

quiz.q: What does the horizontal opening of the eye pattern measure?
quiz.a: The range of sampling instants, in time, over which the eye is still open — that is, the tolerance to timing jitter of the clock recovery circuit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Broadcast and satellite standards such as DVB-S2 offer a small menu of roll-off factors so that operators can trade bandwidth against out-of-band emission. Optical and copper links push α very low and then repair the residual ISI with an equaliser, which is where 5.3 continues. Modern 5G and Wi-Fi use OFDM with a cyclic prefix instead of a raised cosine, but filtered OFDM and filter-bank multicarrier research brings pulse shaping back, because sharp spectrum edges matter when users sit next to each other in frequency. Search for root raised cosine filter design, excess bandwidth, and eye-mask specifications if you want the measurement side.
